sources.title: National Park Service: Hopewell history and culture
sources.note: Direct page, last two paragraphs: network rather than tribe; regional florescence 1 to 400 CE. This narrower Ohio emphasis is used rather than forcing a universal chronology.

sources.title: National Park Service: Ohio’s prehistoric past
sources.note: Direct Middle Woodland section, house construction, middens, bladelets and concluding paragraphs on change by 400 CE and continuing people. No claim that every Hopewell community followed one trajectory.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hopewell farming
sources.note: Direct opening paragraphs: Eastern Agricultural Complex crops, hunting/gathering majority, fields near homes and probable shifting cultivation.

sources.title: National Park Service: archaeological investigations at Hopeton
sources.note: Direct Ongoing Research section: topsoil removal, selected soil layers, burned logs around 300 CE and production pit outside gateway.

sources.title: National Park Service: Seip Earthworks
sources.note: Direct Remarkable Design and Central Mound sections: repeated square dimensions and copper-preserved patterned milkweed textiles. Does not independently prove exact ancient social organization.

sources.title: Ohio History Connection: Newark Earthworks site history
sources.note: Direct lunar-cycle paragraph and material-provenance discussion.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hopewell Mound Group
sources.note: Direct A List of Superlatives: mica hand, copper bear paw, Yellowstone obsidian ceremonial blades; avoid conflicting acreage/height estimates elsewhere on page.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hopewell culture seashells
sources.note: Direct article: lightning-whelk shell cups, columella beads/pendants and ceremonial contexts. Routes and symbolism interpreted, not direct travel records.

sources.title: National Park Service: archaeology at Hopewell Culture
sources.note: Direct opening states no written records of Hopewell culture. No reconstructed language or deciphered symbolic text asserted.

sources.title: Hopi Tribe: official introduction
sources.note: Direct tribal introduction: sovereign nation, northeastern Arizona, twelve villages/three mesas, longstanding farming and continuing language/culture. No implication reservation equals entire ancestral homeland.

sources.title: Michael Kotutwa Johnson: life on a Hopi dryland farm
sources.note: First-person account as told to Kimi Eisele, July 9, 2020. Paragraphs on grandfather, six-to-eighteen-inch planting, spacing, rainfall, women selecting seeds, December stories. Practices explicitly attributed to this farmer.

sources.title: Spencer and Sekaquaptewa: Piki of the Hopi Indians
sources.note: Primary descriptive study, Expedition 37(1), 1995. Piki stone, making piki and uses sections; detailed observations presented as 1995 account, not universal unchanged 1500 practice.

sources.title: Pat Sekaquaptewa: Evolving the Hopi Common Law
sources.note: Author’s account of Hopi governance and customary law. Opening clan and household discussion; no simplified claim that all authority belongs to one gender.

sources.title: National Park Service: Awatovi National Historic Landmark documentation
sources.note: Primary landmark nomination indexed full Statement of Significance:1200 to 1700, contact 1540, mission 1629, revolt 1680, destruction 1700. Current NPS popular page says 1701; draft avoids false year precision by saying around 1700.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Nampeyo bowl E158148
sources.note: Direct/indexed collection catalogue and discussion of 1896 bowl adapting archaeological bird design from Old Cunopavi A157735. Hano Tewa artist attribution retained.

sources.title: Hopi Tribe: tribal government
sources.note: Direct/indexed official page opening: council established 1936, representative powers, village election or kikmongwi appointment. Distinguish 1936 ratification from federal approval; prose only year.

sources.title: Northern Arizona University: Hopi dental hygiene partnership
sources.note: Direct institutional report March 13, 2019. Writing witness askwali and female-speaker translation in coordinator quotation; modern Latin-script reporting. Clinic paired students, assessment, school sealants and screenings.

sources.title: Hopi Tribe: Department of Education and Workforce Development
sources.note: Official departmental mission: Hopi language and culture through school systems and modern technology.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hawikuh and the Zuni-Cibola Complex
sources.note: Direct original-pueblo paragraphs: six multistory blocks, sandstone/adobe, 1200s occupation, 1540 attack and 1629 mission. Some popular accounts conflict on 1670/1672 and final departure; those specific events avoided.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Hawikku jar from Room 172
sources.note: Original catalogue full indexed text: probably A:shiwi attribution, 1630 to 1680 creation, 1920 excavation, Room 172 House Group F, coiled/painted/glazed. Direct fetch failed; collection date not misused as manufacture date.

sources.title: Zuni Tribal Archives: Old Zuni Mission
sources.note: Original tribal archive indexed full cultural narrative; direct 502. Checked 1680 revolt and 1700 reestablishment; founding-date disagreement with HABS excluded.

sources.title: University of Michigan: Zuni waffle-garden photograph, about 1912
sources.note: Primary museum photograph catalogue (record 160, slide 18212), full indexed description. Image restricted; review relies on catalogue description of women planting and small depressions holding bucket-carried river water.

sources.title: Zuni Youth Enrichment Project: families conserve rainwater
sources.note: Organization’s August 2, 2021 program report. 100 families, 88 barrels, 12 gutter kits, utility partnership; all figures fixed to report year.

sources.title: Zuni Youth Enrichment Project: food sovereignty
sources.note: Direct program account: waffle-garden teaching, youth internships and middle-school cooking class. No broad health-cure claims borrowed.

sources.title: A:shiwi A:wan Museum: exhibitions
sources.note: Original museum page full indexed text; direct timeout. Hawikku 2002 loan 221 objects; Day School 1898 to 1965; Map Art 16 artists 31 works. Budget combines all passages attributed to this URL.

sources.title: A:shiwi A:wan Museum: contact page
sources.note: Original museum indexed page closes with Elahkwa and explicit English Thank you. Undated modern community web witness, not ancient script. Direct page failed.

sources.title: Pueblo of Zuni: A:shiwi A:wan Messenger, issue 21
sources.note: Primary tribal newsletter indexed ZYEP Unveils Zuni Turkey Maiden Film section, February 2022. Archive stories recorded 1960s, 2019 first stage performance, 2022 broadcast. Direct PDF fetch failed; exact indexed paragraph checked.

sources.title: Pueblo of Zuni: official tribal election information
sources.note: Official 2026 page documents continuing governor, lieutenant governor, council and electoral institutions; no future outcome predicted.

sources.title: Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History: Chumash daily life
sources.note: Direct museum text, Canoes, Shelter, Sweathouse and Cooking sections. Four concise passages together remain below 200 words. Museum distinguishes historical descriptions from present-day practice.

sources.title: National Park Service: Chumash on Anacapa Island
sources.note: Direct opening archaeological paragraph and historic homeland section. Seasonal occupation is an interpretation from water availability, not certainty; do not borrow dubious early tomol chronology elsewhere on page.

sources.title: UC Santa Barbara: Lynn Gamble on an ancient shell-bead economy
sources.note: Direct university interview with study author, January 28, 2021. Early currency interpretation explicitly attributed to Gamble, based on labor, standardization and distribution; avoid universal first-money claim.

sources.title: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians: our history
sources.note: Direct tribal account of village society, women chiefs, Spanish expedition in 1769, missions, epidemics and 1834 secularization. Modern nation perspective not substituted for all Chumash groups.

sources.title: National Park Service: Mission Santa Inés and the Chumash Revolt
sources.note: Direct final paragraph: Mexican independence in 1821, forced work and IOU payment, beating in February 1824 sparking revolt. Colonial regimes kept distinct.

sources.title: National Park Service: Chumash tomol crossing
sources.note: Direct specific September 11, 2004 crossing account: 21 miles, over ten hours, youth aged 14 to 22. Not using same page’s first-tomol-in-142-years claim, contradicted by museum’s 1913 Librado vessel.

sources.title: Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians: culture and language programs
sources.note: Direct program origins in 2008, six apprentices, expansion in 2013; basket and cooking workshops; living cultural institutions.

sources.title: Santa Ynez Band: Samala magazine, November to December 2022
sources.note: Direct full PDF. Publication identity printed page 2; exact greeting and translation printed page 5/PDF index 4; language-at-home curriculum same page. Original apostrophe retained in haku tikaliʼ. Modern Samala witness, not a precolonial inscription.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Verified missing and reserved. Decoded world 1492 polygon bbox -86.3379 to -81.3122, 37.5350 to 40.6290; imported 1492 to 1500 is a serious chronological error for Ohio Hopewell. Public overview explicitly rejects contemporary-state reading. Narrative focuses regional 1 to 400 CE florescence supported by current NPS rather than attributing broad 200 BCE to 500 CE to all examples. No alias to Adena or later historic nations; no tribal extinction or invented writing.

Verified missing and reserved. Decoded world 1500 polygon bbox -116.6322 to -108.6941, 30.0725 to 36.4102 is grossly oversized southwest of northeastern Arizona; opening flags Baja-directed extension. No neighboring peoples absorbed. Map 1500 to 1530 does not determine historical lifetime. Modern sources explicitly date farmer 2020, piki 1995, clinic 2019. Awatovi 1700/1701 source discrepancy handled around 1700. Nampeyo identified Hopi-Tewa; general Hopi community identity does not erase Tewa distinction.

Verified missing, no staged collision. Index 1530 to 1650; first decoded world 1530 polygon bbox -109.4573 to -108.3269, 34.4802 to 35.3704 correctly in western New Mexico but not exhaustive ancestral cultural landscape. No alias to neighboring Pueblo nations. Individual Hawikku abandonment not equated to Zuni ending. Halona mission-source founding chronology disagreement excluded; 1680 revolt and circa 1700 rebuilding used. All modern practice examples dates or sections distinguish from imported interval. Museum writing exact indexed community witness.

Verified missing with no staged collision. Index 1492 to 1650; decoded first outline bbox -121.1286 to -118.1118, 33.9199 to 35.6770 covers California coast. Regional cultural label, not a single centralized empire or all present-day nations merged. Homeland narrative includes northern islands without asserting exact polygon precision. Santa Ynez examples are explicitly community-specific. Modern Samala writing sample directly checked on the tribal magazine printed page 5. Historical period after map endpoint deliberately explains later disruption and continuity. Excluded conflicting NPS statement that 1976 saw the first tomol in 142 years, since the museum records Fernando Librado’s 1913 vessel.
